title: Measured Throughput, Inter-Packet Latency, Flow Direction & Traffic Patterns
topic: Throughput, Latency, Packet Loss, Active Connections, Traffic Direction, Utilization
learning_objectives: Measure real application goodput/throughput (KB/s, Mbps), packet counts, and duration from live captured executions.
Analyze directional byte totals (client->server vs. server->client) and multi-flow traffic patterns.
Distinguish header overhead vs. application payload (goodput vs. wire throughput) and identify anomalies like RSTs or retransmissions.

concept_explanation.title: Throughput, Goodput & Latency Metrics
concept_explanation.summary: Network monitoring quantifies real link and flow performance: wire throughput includes L2/L3/L4 headers, goodput counts only application payload bytes per second, and latency measures round-trip or inter-packet delay.
key_points: Small frequent writes incur higher header-to-payload overhead than larger batched transfers.
Always compute metrics strictly from measured monotonic timestamps and byte counts — never fabricated dashboards.

concept_explanation.title: Flow Direction & Anomaly Detection
concept_explanation.summary: Monitoring tools group packets into bidirectional flows to observe asymmetry (e.g., downloads vs. echoes), connection spikes, unexpected RST packets, and retransmission candidates.
key_points: Comparing packets_a_to_b vs. packets_b_to_a and payload bytes reveals traffic symmetry.
Sudden RST bursts or repeated sequence numbers signal crashes, firewall drops, or congestion.

experiment.title: Monitor a Live Multi-Chunk TCP Data Transfer & Multi-Flow Pattern
experiment.instructions: Executes a controlled localhost bulk TCP transfer (multiple chunks totaling ~64 KB) under LD_PRELOAD + libpcap, computing real measured duration, wire bytes, application goodput, inter-packet latency stats, and directional flow symmetry.
required_setup: Phase 2 LD_PRELOAD tracer & Phase 4 libpcap capture helper
execution_steps: Run 'Measured Bulk TCP Transfer (~64 KB)' and review the real measured throughput, goodput, packet count, and min/avg/max inter-packet interval.
Compare against 'Multiple Concurrent TCP Flows' (Module 4/9) to see how multiple flows share loopback.
Ask the Grounded Local AI Assistant to interpret the measured flow balance and packet timing.

supported_scenarios.label: 1. Measured Bulk TCP Transfer (~64 KB Goodput & Latency)
supported_scenarios.description: Transfers 16 x 4096-byte chunks over loopback TCP and computes real measured wire/payload throughput and inter-packet timing.

supported_scenarios.label: 2. Multi-Flow Concurrent Traffic Pattern
supported_scenarios.description: Runs 2 concurrent TCP flows to compare per-flow packet counts and directional payload symmetry.

expected_observations: Measured wire bytes exceed application payload bytes due to IPv4 + TCP headers.
Echo traffic exhibits symmetric payload bytes in client->server and server->client directions.
All throughput and inter-packet latency figures derive strictly from real monotonic timestamps.
observation_caveats: Loopback throughput reflects host memory/kernel copy speed, not physical Wi-Fi or Ethernet link speed.
Monotonic libpcap callback timestamps measure host capture time rather than hardware NIC timestamps.

questions.prompt: Why is measured wire throughput always slightly higher than application-layer goodput for a TCP transfer?
options: Because TCP compresses application payloads automatically.
Because wire bytes include Ethernet/IPv4/TCP headers and control packets (SYN/ACK/FIN) in addition to application payload bytes.
Because loopback doubles every payload byte.
questions.rubric_summary: Wire throughput includes protocol headers and control packets; goodput counts only useful application payload.
questions.explanation: Goodput measures useful application payload delivered per unit time, excluding L2/L3/L4 header overhead and control/retransmitted segments.

questions.prompt: If a TCP flow transfers 65,536 bytes of payload in 0.010 seconds (10 ms), what is the approximate application goodput?
questions.explanation: Dividing 65,536 bytes by 0.01 seconds yields 6,553,600 bytes/sec (~6.55 MB/s), or ~52.4 megabits per second.

questions.prompt: Why might a network monitoring alert flag a sudden spike in TCP RST packets or duplicate sequence numbers on a production link?
questions.rubric_summary: RST spikes indicate abrupt crashes/firewall blocks/port scans; duplicate seq numbers indicate packet loss/retransmissions.
questions.explanation: Unexpected RST bursts indicate crashed processes, active firewall resets, or scans against closed ports; repeated sequence numbers indicate possible retransmissions caused by packet loss or congestion.
